Mary knows every physical fact about color vision before she ever sees color. When she sees red, Jackson’s original claim is that she learns a new fact, so complete physical knowledge did not give her all the facts. (Jackson, 1982, 1986)
the reply menu:

ability reply: Mary gains a new ability, such as recognizing and imagining red, rather than a new fact. (Lewis, 1988; Nemirow, 1990)
acquaintance reply: Mary gains direct acquaintance with red experience, rather than a new public fact.
phenomenal concept reply: Mary gains a first-person concept for a fact she already knew physically. (Loar, 1990)
Jackson later backs away from the anti-physicalist conclusion. (Jackson, 1998)

what this note tests is completeness. If a finished physical theory leaves Mary ignorant of what red is like, physicalism owes a story that explains the ignorance without adding a new nonphysical fact.bibliographieJackson, F. (1982).
